items.prompt: What do a 40-page wiki dump and 'just look around and ask questions' have in common?
choices: Both give the new hire far too little to read
Neither anchors the material to a task
Both rely on a buddy answering every question
items.explanation: Each hands over unstructured material without an anchoring task.

items.prompt: What is onboarding, in this unit's framing?
choices: Handing over the documents and then waiting for results
A one-time orientation meeting held on the first day
Getting someone new productive, by deliberate design
items.explanation: It is a design problem, not a document handover.

items.prompt: What is cognitive overload in this unit?
choices: Too much unanchored information arriving at once
A new hire working too many hours in the first week
A task too hard for the person's current skills
items.explanation: The problem is information with nothing to connect to.

items.prompt: Tomas read all 40 pages as asked. Was the plan careless?
choices: Yes, he should have started shipping on his own
No; the order of the plan was the flaw
Yes, the wiki had clearly been written badly
items.explanation: He followed the plan; the plan put reading before doing.

items.prompt: What is a ramp plan?
choices: A fixed reading list covering the whole system
A schedule of weekly meetings with the manager
A sequence of growing tasks that builds context gradually
items.explanation: It sequences tasks, not documents.

items.prompt: How does a ramp plan treat context?
choices: It introduces it when the next task needs it
It delivers all of it on the first day
It withholds it until the new hire asks
items.explanation: Context is pulled in by the work.

items.prompt: Why can a dump fail even when it is read in full?
choices: People cannot read that many pages in two weeks
Nothing in it is connected to current work yet
New hires rarely take written material seriously
items.explanation: Reading completed is not the same as context retained.

items.prompt: 'Look around and ask questions' is best described as...
choices: A gentler version of a ramp plan with less pressure
A way of granting real autonomy to a new hire
The same missing structure, from the other side
items.explanation: With no starting task, exploration has no direction.

items.prompt: A manager replaces the 40-page wiki with a 10-page one, keeping 'read it, then we talk in two weeks'. What is the most accurate verdict?
choices: Fixed, because page volume was the actual cause of the stall
Worse, because less material leaves the new hire guessing more
Shorter, but still reading first, so the root cause remains
Neutral, because page count and outcomes are unrelated here
items.explanation: The failure was the order, reading before doing. Trimming pages shortens the delay but keeps the order.
items.reference:
Two failures, one cause
40-page dump: nothing tied to a task
'look around and ask': no starting point
ramp plan: small real task + the context it needs
Why: both leave the new hire guessing what matters now; only a task gives the material somewhere to attach.
items.learnMore:
Reading first, doing later

A dump and a vacuum look like opposites, but both hand over unstructured material and expect the new hire to sort out relevance alone. What is missing is an anchor: a task that tells them which parts matter today.

Common mistake

Believing a better or shorter document would have rescued the plan.
items.reflection: Think of a time you were handed a pile of material at the start of something new. What would have made it stick sooner?

items.prompt: Hire A gets full repository access and 'explore'. Hire B gets 40 pages to read. Which statement holds?
choices: Both lack an anchoring task, so both stall for the same reason
A is better off, because exploring beats reading in every case
B is better off, because the pages at least give some direction
Neither stalls, since each is free to learn at their own pace
items.explanation: Access and pages are both unstructured material; neither says what matters first.

choices: Smart people absorb a dump quickly, so a longer wiki would work better
The approach works as long as the manager checks in every two weeks
They still need a scoped task to know what comes first
Access alone is enough as long as the codebase is well documented
items.explanation: Intelligence speeds learning but does not tell anyone which part of a large system to learn first.

items.prompt: What does time-to-first-contribution measure?
choices: How many pages of material they have covered
How many questions they ask in the first week
Days until a new hire ships something real
items.explanation: It is about shipping, not reading.

items.prompt: By day 14, what had Tomas shipped?
choices: Nothing
A typo fix
A small bug
items.explanation: He had read everything and shipped nothing.

items.prompt: Is coverage the same as time-to-first-contribution?
choices: Yes, both rise together as someone reads more
No, coverage counts what was given, not what was done
Yes, coverage is the same measure counted in pages
items.explanation: They measure different things.

items.prompt: Could a hire cover 100% of the material and still have a poor time-to-first-contribution?
choices: No, full coverage guarantees an early first ship
No, the two always move in the same direction
Yes, reading and shipping are separate things
items.explanation: Tomas is exactly this case.

items.prompt: Why does a first contribution count even if it is small?
choices: Any real ship shows the ramp is moving
Only large features are worth counting
Small changes are never reviewed by anyone
items.explanation: The signal is that real work has flowed through the team.

items.prompt: Who is an onboarding buddy?
choices: A second manager who runs weekly check-ins
A teammate, not the manager, for quick questions
Another new hire who started the same week
items.explanation: The buddy is a low-overhead question channel.

items.prompt: Which is a warning sign that the ramp may be failing?
choices: The new hire asks many small questions
The new hire is working on a small first task
Two weeks pass with nothing real shipped
items.explanation: Questions and small tasks are healthy; silence in shipping is not.

items.prompt: What does time-to-first-contribution tell you?
choices: Whether the plan is working, not why it is failing
Exactly which section of the plan went wrong
How talented the new hire is overall
items.explanation: It is a signal, so finding the cause needs further looking.

items.prompt: Two new hires finish all assigned reading in week 1. Hire A ships a fix on day 3; hire B ships nothing by day 14. What can be concluded?
choices: Hire B probably read less carefully than hire A did
Hire A was given an easier role than hire B was
Both ramps are equal, since the coverage is the same
Coverage is equal; only hire A's ramp is working
items.explanation: Equal coverage with different shipping shows coverage was never the right measure.
items.reference:
Coverage vs. contribution
coverage: pages read, checklist items done
time-to-first-contribution: days until something real ships
Tomas: 100% coverage, 0 shipped at day 14
Why: coverage counts what was given; time-to-first-contribution shows what the new hire can actually do.
items.learnMore:
A signal, not a diagnosis

Time-to-first-contribution is easy to observe and hard to fake. It tells you whether the ramp is moving, but not which part of the plan is responsible when it is not.

Common mistake

Reporting onboarding as healthy because a checklist is complete.
items.reflection: Where in your own work do you track what was covered instead of what was delivered? What would the delivery version look like?

items.prompt: A manager reports 'onboarding is on track: 100% of the checklist is done'. What is the most useful follow-up question?
choices: Can the checklist be made longer next time?
What has the new hire shipped, and when?
How many pages does the wiki contain now?
Did the new hire enjoy working through the checklist?
items.explanation: Completion is about inputs; shipping is the outcome the plan exists to produce.

choices: The new hire is certainly more talented than the last
Each part of the redesign worked equally well
Nothing, because a single number tells you nothing
The ramp improved, but not which change caused it
items.explanation: The metric shows direction, not attribution.

items.prompt: What follows the first small task once it ships?
choices: Progressively larger tasks with more autonomy
A full read-through of the whole wiki, start to end
A final evaluation of the new hire's results
items.explanation: Scope grows with the new hire's context.

items.prompt: What does day 1 of a ramp plan contain?
choices: A 40-page reading list, then a two-week gap
Setup, one small real task, a named buddy
A company-wide tour of every system and team
items.explanation: Day 1 is about starting, not studying.

items.prompt: Does the first real task wait until the system has been studied?
choices: Yes, the study must be finished before starting
Yes, but only the first half of the wiki
No, the task comes first and pulls the study in
items.explanation: Study is driven by the task.

items.prompt: Why does context that arrives just in time work better?
choices: It is used straight away, so it sticks
It reduces how much context is needed overall
It lets the manager skip explaining anything
items.explanation: Use right after arrival is what makes it stick.

items.prompt: What happens to context introduced with no use for it?
choices: It stays fully available for later in the same form
Little is retained, since nothing connects to it
It speeds up the first real task regardless
items.explanation: Unanchored information fades.

items.prompt: What role does the wiki play in a ramp plan?
choices: It is deleted, since documents do not help
It is the day-1 assignment, as before
Sections are read when a task touches that area
items.explanation: It is still useful, just not first.

items.prompt: In the unit's model (0.35 days of delay per page), what do 20 pages before any task cost?
choices: About 7 days
About 14 days
About 2 days
items.explanation: 20 pages times 0.35 is 7 days.

items.prompt: What is the 30/60/90 checkpoint for?
choices: Handing over the full wiki in three installments
Comparing actual progress with the plan's expectation
Reviewing the quality of the wiki pages
items.explanation: It checks the plan against reality.

items.prompt: A team's plan has week 1 for reading the architecture docs and week 2 for the first task. Which change fixes the root cause with the least disruption?
choices: Give the first small task now and attach the docs to it
Shorten the docs and keep reading first in week 1
Add a second week of reading before the first task
Replace the docs with a recorded walkthrough video
items.explanation: The order must change; content and format changes keep reading ahead of doing.
items.reference:
What a ramp plan sequences
day 1: setup + one small real task + buddy
week 1: ship it, see review in practice
weeks 2-4: larger tasks, less hand-holding
30/60/90: plan vs. actual
Why: the work comes first and pulls the context in, so every piece of context is used soon after it arrives.
items.learnMore:
Just enough, just in time

Each stage gives the new hire one step more than they can currently do, plus the context that step needs. The wiki stays useful, but a section is read when a task touches that area.

Common mistake

Treating a shortened reading list as if it were a ramp plan.
items.reflection: Pick something you recently learned well. Was the reading before the doing, or the other way round, and which stuck better?

items.prompt: In the unit's model (0.35 days per page, rounded), only 10 of the 40 pages must precede the first task and 30 move behind it. Roughly how long until the first contribution?
choices: About 11 days, the delay from the 30 pages that moved
About 14 days, since the total reading is unchanged
About 4 days, since 10 pages times 0.35 rounds to 4
About 1 day, since moved reading costs nothing at all
items.explanation: Only reading before the task delays it: 10 times 0.35 is 3.5, about 4 days.

items.prompt: Why add a buddy alongside the manager?
choices: Reporting on the new hire to the manager
Small questions that cannot wait
Taking over the new hire's first task
items.explanation: The buddy serves a different cadence.

items.prompt: What is the manager check-in's cadence?
choices: Immediate and informal
Continuous and always on call
Scheduled and infrequent
items.explanation: That cadence is why a second channel is needed.

items.prompt: Who answers a two-minute config question best?
choices: The buddy, right away
The manager, at the next check-in
Nobody, so the new hire guesses
items.explanation: Low overhead is the buddy's whole purpose.

items.prompt: When are small questions most frequent?
choices: Right before the 90-day mark
In the early days of the role
Only after the first task ships
items.explanation: Everything is unfamiliar at the start.

items.prompt: What does saving small questions for the check-in cost?
choices: The manager's calendar becomes too empty
The buddy loses track of the new hire
The task blocks or gets a guess
items.explanation: Waiting either stops work or invites guesses.

items.prompt: What is the manager best used for in onboarding?
choices: Direction, priorities, and checking the plan
Answering each small how-do-I question
Replacing the buddy whenever it is busy
items.explanation: Their time goes to decisions only they can make.

items.prompt: Is the buddy the new hire's manager?
choices: Yes, a second manager for the first month
No, a teammate with no authority over them
Yes, but only for technical questions
items.explanation: That is what makes asking cheap.

items.prompt: Why did Tomas's gap grow unnoticed for two weeks?
choices: His manager checked in on him too often
He was given too small a first task
He had no low-overhead place to take questions
items.explanation: Only a rare check-in existed.

items.prompt: At 10am a new hire wonders which service owns retry logic; the manager check-in is Thursday. What is the best path?
choices: Wait for Thursday so the manager sees all the gaps
Ask the buddy now; keep the check-in for direction
Guess from the code and mention it Thursday if wrong
Post to the whole team channel and skip the buddy
items.explanation: A quick answer unblocks work, and the check-in remains for what only the manager decides.
items.reference:
Two channels, two jobs
manager: scheduled, infrequent: direction, priorities, plan checks
buddy: immediate, informal: small 'what does this mean' questions
Tomas: only the first, and a 14-day gap
Why: small questions need a low-overhead path or they block work or get answered by guessing.
items.learnMore:
Questions have a cadence

The early weeks generate many small questions. A scheduled channel cannot serve them, so a named teammate with permission to be interrupted absorbs them and leaves the manager's time for decisions only the manager can make.

Common mistake

Assuming 'ask me anything' from a busy manager is the same as an available channel.
items.reflection: Who was your quick-question person when you last started something new? What would you have done without them?

items.prompt: A manager says 'my door is always open, so a buddy is redundant'. What is the main weakness?
choices: Managers are never able to answer technical questions
A buddy gives the manager an extra person to supervise
New hires are always too shy to approach an open door
Each question still costs an interruption, so small ones go unasked
items.explanation: The open door lowers the barrier but not to the level of a peer who expects questions.

They will not be able to read the new hire's code
items.explanation: A buddy only helps if answering quickly is actually possible for them.

items.prompt: Why must the first task be real?
choices: It is the only kind the manager is able to grade
It guarantees the new hire never makes errors
It teaches the real code, review, and norms
items.explanation: Realness is what teaches the system.

items.prompt: What does environment setup on day 1 confirm?
choices: That the tools work before harder work relies on them
That the new hire has already read the whole wiki
That the real task is small enough to finish
items.explanation: A broken setup is better found early and cheaply.

items.prompt: What makes a good first task?
choices: Large and open-ended to show initiative
Small, real, and scoped with a clear definition of done
Fake but safe, built just for onboarding
items.explanation: It must be finishable and testable.

items.prompt: Why a typo fix on day 1?
choices: It is the real first task of the plan
It replaces the need for any later review
A quick check that setup works
items.explanation: It is a tooling check, not the task.

items.prompt: What does a sandbox exercise teach?
choices: The tools, but not how the real system works
Everything a real task teaches, but more safely
Only the team's review norms
items.explanation: It lacks the real code and process.

items.prompt: Shipping something real is a trust signal for whom?
choices: Only the new hire's own confidence
Both the new hire and the team
Only the manager's reporting
items.explanation: Each side sees how the other works.

items.prompt: Why should the first task be scoped?
choices: It keeps the task from needing any review
It makes having a buddy unnecessary
It can be done with a fraction of the full context
items.explanation: Scoping limits what must be learned first.

items.prompt: Which is a real, small, scoped task?
choices: A well-defined bug fix in one file with a test
A rewrite of a core service's architecture
A fake bug in a throwaway practice repo
items.explanation: It is real, finishable, and verifiable.

items.prompt: A manager proposes a standalone demo app that mirrors team patterns but is unconnected to production. What is the best assessment?
choices: It is equivalent to a real task and far safer to run
It is better than a real task, since failure costs nothing
It teaches patterns but skips real review and owners
It is useless, because demo apps teach nothing about tools
items.explanation: Useful practice, but the system-specific learning needs real work.
items.reference:
Real vs. built-for-onboarding
sandbox exercise: teaches tools only
small real task: tools + code + review + norms
trust signal: weak vs. both directions
Why: a real task teaches the system as a side effect of completing it, which no toy can imitate.
items.learnMore:
Small, real, scoped

Each word matters. Small and scoped keep the task finishable on a fraction of the context; real means the new hire passes through the actual code, review and norms on the way.

Common mistake

Choosing the safest task possible and losing the part that teaches.
items.reflection: Think of a first real task you were given anywhere. What did completing it teach you that a practice version would not have?

items.prompt: Which candidate best fits as a first task?
choices: A bug in one module with a failing test to turn green
Redesigning the logging pipeline to learn the whole system
Summarising the architecture to prove understanding of it
Building a to-do app to practise the team's tooling
items.explanation: It is small, real, scoped, and has an unambiguous done.

choices: Keep it, since a real task needs real depth
Swap it for a sandbox exercise needing fewer systems
Re-scope it to touch fewer systems while keeping it real
Give the new hire the wiki sections for all five
items.explanation: The problem is scope, so fix scope without losing the realness.

items.prompt: Does an experienced hire need a ramp plan?
choices: Yes, but aimed at different gaps
No, experience replaces the plan
Yes, identical to a new graduate's plan
items.explanation: The need remains; the target shifts.

items.prompt: What do experienced hires usually lack?
choices: Basic skill at writing and reading everyday code
Org context: who decides, what is fragile
The ability to work without any direction at all
items.explanation: They bring skill but not this team's map.

items.prompt: Which part usually needs less hand-holding for them?
choices: Knowing who owns each system and service
Learning which areas of the code are fragile
The technical execution of the first task
items.explanation: They reason about unfamiliar code quickly.

items.prompt: What does unanchored information do for an experienced person?
choices: It does not stick for them either
It sticks fine because they know more
It sticks only if it is technical
items.explanation: The mechanism does not depend on seniority of skill.

items.prompt: Skipping the plan because of experience recreates...
choices: A faster ramp with no downsides
The original mistake in a different costume
The buddy relationship in a new form
items.explanation: Unstructured access is still unstructured.

items.prompt: Why can early missteps look like confidence?
choices: They tend to ignore feedback altogether
Their tasks are always the riskiest ones
Fast output hides the missing map
items.explanation: Speed masks the gap.

items.prompt: Where does an experienced hire's plan lean?
choices: Owners, decision history, fragile areas
More technical pairing sessions on the codebase
A much longer reading list of technical material
items.explanation: That is the information they lack.

items.prompt: Which question is about org context?
choices: How does this language handle null values?
Which team must be told before changing this?
What does this library function return?
items.explanation: The other two are technical.

items.prompt: An experienced hire declines the plan and gets full access. Two weeks in they refactor a module another team depends on, unaware. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Poor technical judgement that hiring should have caught
Too little autonomy during the first two weeks
Too much structure during the first two weeks
An org-context gap that the plan would have covered early
items.explanation: The change was probably well made; the missing piece was whom it affects.
items.reference:
Where the plan leans
new engineer: technical hand-holding on the task
experienced hire: owners, fragile areas, decision history
both: scoped task, just-in-time context, a buddy
Why: the mechanism is the same for everyone; what changes is which gap the structure fills.
items.learnMore:
Skill is not a map

Experience supplies technical speed but not this team's decisions, owners or history. The same plan, retargeted at that gap, protects against fast, confident, and unintentionally risky early changes.

Common mistake

Reading a fast start as proof that no structure is needed.
items.reflection: Think of someone highly skilled who joined a group you were in. What did they not yet know that skill could not give them?

items.prompt: Which adjustment best retargets the plan for an experienced hire?
choices: Drop the scoped task and assign a large project instead
Keep a scoped task; add owners and decision history
Keep the plan but add pairing on basic syntax and tools
Drop the buddy, as they will find answers alone quickly
items.explanation: Structure stays; its content moves toward what they lack.

Why: the mechanism is the same for everyone; what changes is which gap the structure fills.

Experience supplies technical speed but not this team's decisions, owners or history. The same plan, retargeted at that gap, protects against fast, confident, and unintentionally risky early changes.

items.prompt: Why might a manager wrongly judge an experienced hire as fine at day 14?
choices: Experienced people tend to ship fewer tasks than they could
Experienced people ask more questions than needed
Fast output is simply unrelated to onboarding success overall
Fast technical output masks the missing map of the org
items.explanation: Shipping speed is a signal that can hide a context gap.

items.prompt: What happens at each 30/60/90 mark?
choices: The plan is fixed and nothing is revisited
Actual progress is compared with the plan
The wiki is re-read from the start
items.explanation: It is a comparison with an option to adjust.

items.prompt: Is a ramp plan a fixed script?
choices: Yes, any deviation shows the hire is weak
Yes, changing it breaks the buddy's role
No, a starting structure to adjust
items.explanation: It is a hypothesis about one person.

items.prompt: A new hire is ahead of plan at 30 days. A sensible adjustment?
choices: Resize upcoming tasks larger
Pause tasks until the plan catches up
Cancel the 60-day checkpoint
items.explanation: Match the plan to the person.

items.prompt: A new hire is behind plan at 30 days. A sensible response?
choices: Keep the plan unchanged and wait it out
Find the gap and resize tasks or add support
Add a much longer reading list for the hire
items.explanation: Look for the cause before adjusting.

items.prompt: What does the 60-day mark compare?
choices: Pages read against the wiki's total length
Pay against the original offer
Autonomy against how much buddy help is still needed
items.explanation: It checks whether the buddy can taper.

items.prompt: What is the 90-day mark about?
choices: Ownership of an area, then next goals
Starting the first real task of the plan
Assigning the new hire a buddy for help
items.explanation: Ramp-up is ending and the next phase begins.

items.prompt: Why check at all if the plan was carefully made?
choices: Plans written on day 1 are always wrong
It is a guess about one person's pace
Checkpoints keep the manager's calendar busy
items.explanation: Observation replaces assumption.

items.prompt: What does a script that ignores progress miss?
choices: Nothing; adjusting only adds noise
The need for any first task at all
A gap opening up that a checkpoint would catch
items.explanation: Fixed plans cannot react.

items.prompt: At 30 days a new hire has shipped three tasks against the plan's one and asks few questions. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Resize upcoming tasks and bring autonomy goals forward
Hold to the plan, since deviation signals a risk to manage
Cut tasks back to match the plan's original pace exactly
Skip the 60-day checkpoint, as it no longer applies here
items.explanation: Ahead of plan is information; the plan should follow the person.
items.reference:
30 / 60 / 90
30: tasks shipped vs. plan: resize tasks
60: autonomy vs. buddy help needed: taper or extend
90: ownership of an area: set next goals
Why: a plan is a guess about one person's pace; checkpoints replace the guess with observation.
items.learnMore:
Plan vs. observation

Each checkpoint asks a different question, and each can change the plan. The value is in the adjustment, not in the meeting happening on the calendar.

Common mistake

Holding the original plan fixed when the person is clearly ahead or behind.
items.reflection: Think of a plan you made and never revisited. What did a checkpoint, if you had held one, have the chance to catch?

items.prompt: At 60 days the plan expected the buddy's role to taper, but the new hire still needs them for most tasks. What is the best response?

Conclude the hire is a poor fit and stop supporting
Find which area drives the dependence and add targeted support
Wait until 90 days before saying anything
items.explanation: A dependence usually points to a specific gap, which can be addressed.
